newsitem.title: UK: Airbus seeks broader European grouping.
newsitem.headline: Airbus seeks broader European grouping.

text.p: The Airbus Industrie consortium said on Friday it was trying to bring other European aircraft makers into its plans to transform its four-nation industry and state cooperative structure into an autonomous corporation.

"I am devoting all my energies to winning over the other European manufacturers -- that is, our Italian friends Alenia and our Swedish friends Saab -- to participate in this new partnership," Manfred Bischoff, head of member company Daimler Aerospace, told the Financial Times World Aerospace and Air Transport Conference.
Bischoff said the other three Airbus members, British Aerospace Plc, France's Aerospatiale and Spain's CASA, were also busy trying to recruit the two firms.

The consortium and the Airbus operations in each member company are to be merged before the end of the century "to form a single company with profits being the full responsibility of the management", Bischoff said.
He said he was not discounting the political and industrial obstacles that would lie in the way of this corporate aim but added: "We cannot have Europeanisation free of charge."
Among these obstacles he included job cuts and cost rationalisation.
"To achieve a greater efficiency and new cost structures we will have to pay the price of trimming the workforce, for example," he said.

"In addition, we will have to work out a comprehensive accommodation of conflicting interests that reconcile national interests, and existing national (manufacturing and workshare) positions, with our jointly-agreed corporate objectives."

Bischoff added that a potential conflict of interest between privately-owned companies such as BAe, Daimler and Saab and state-owned enterprises like Aerospatiale, Alenia and CASA could be resolved by way of privatisation.
"We must also cut back the role of government to that of purely shareholder," he told the conference, adding that privatisation was by no means the only option.
Meanwhile, plans are afoot for Airbus to take over a proposal by a three-nation European consortium to build a new 100-seat regional jet in partnership with China and a company from Singapore.

Mike Turner, chairman of commercial aerospace for British Aerospace, told the conference that while BAe and its partners Alenia and Aerospatiale in the AI(R) consortium had successfully negotiated an exclusive Memorandum of Understanding with the Far Eastern partners, there was still a great deal of work to do to get to a launch decision.
"Included in that work has to be the transfer of the programme from our AI(R) partnership into Airbus," he said.
"Without Airbus we do not see the required market to justify the launch of such a programme. This view is shared by both our Chinese and Singaporean partners.
"BAe's position is that the aircraft have to be part of the Airbus family and we therefore have to bring Germany and Spain into the 100-seater project," he added.
"Clearly this also involves the entry of Italy, through Alenia, into the Airbus consortium".
